title: Police officer\'s bid to seal interview on fatal hotel shooting fails
subtitle: Anthony Heffernan\'s family has been sharply critical of what they call the lack of transparency and accountability from police in the controversial shooting of their loved one
article: A Calgary police officer\'s attempt to have an interview regarding the fatal shooting of a man in a city hotel withheld from a review board has been rejected.

Const. Robert Brauer had argued releasing compelled statements he made into the 2015 shooting of Anthony Heffernan by a police colleague to the Alberta Law Enforcement Review Board (LERB) was unconstitutional.
But the LERB dismissed his application, ruling the officer\'s statements don\'t have immunity under the province\'s Police Act.

"Section 20 (of the Police Act) gives the board the authority to require a chief of police to produce to the board, prior to an appeal hearing, copies of all investigative reports, statements, correspondence or other documents or things relating to the matter," concluded the three-person LERB panel in its Feb. 6 decision.
"The board will proceed to a hearing where the parties\' submissions on whether the board should admit the interviews as part of the record will be considered by the board."
Family critical of alleged lack of transparency, accountability
Heffernan\'s family has been sharply critical of what they call the lack of transparency and accountability from police in the controversial shooting of their loved one.
They\'ve made an appeal to the LERB after filing complaints with the CPS over the shooting they contend was unnecessary.

On March 16, 2015, four officers, including Brauer, entered Anthony Heffernan\'s room at the Super 8 Motel - at 3030 Barlow Trail N.E. - after a staffer had reported he wasn\'t answering requests to check out.
The officers said it appeared the man had been using drugs and was acting aggressively toward them.
Officer wasn\'t charged in Heffernan\'s death
Heffernan, 27, was shot and killed by Const. Maurice McLoughlin, who the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team recommended be charged in his death.
But Alberta Crown prosecutors declined to lay charges, saying there wasn\'t enough evidence to convict.
And in his own review of the case, Calgary police Chief Mark Neufeld said because McLoughlin resigned from the service last May, he can no longer be disciplined.

In its Feb. 6 ruling, the LERB noted it had notified the parties in the case in January 2022 that it believed officers had control over directed explanatory reports but not over directed interviews, such as Brauer\'s, who should then provide them with copies by Jan. 21 of last year.
LERB says Brauer\'s challenge not relevant, premature

That\'s when Brauer launched his constitutional challenge, arguing that in this case, the provision of the Police Act cited by the LERB should have no effect and that the board lacks jurisdiction when determining law related to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
But the LERB determined the argument isn\'t relevant because it doesn\'t involve the possible loss "of life, liberty and security of the person" as required under the charter.
It also said Brauer\'s challenge is premature because it\'s not known how the LERB would use his statements.
"The mere production of the directed statements to the board does not automatically mean that the statements will be used against the respondent officers for a criminal purpose," stated the LERB.

"The board takes the view that in order to be in a position to decide if one or more of the respondent officers\' actions may constitute a federal or provincial offence, the directed statements need to be admitted into the record."
